Mechanistic interpretability asks whether we can reverse-engineer the algorithms implemented by neural network weights — not just what a model outputs, but how it computes it. Attention heads are a natural unit of analysis because they're relatively localized, but the central puzzle in attention head superposition is that a transformer may be implementing more functional roles than it has heads: individual heads appear to polysemantically encode multiple distinct algorithmic operations depending on context, much like how superposition in MLP layers lets neurons represent more features than dimensions. The key concepts to hold simultaneously are superposition (the geometry of how a model packs more representations than it has dimensions, exploiting near-orthogonality in high-dimensional space), circuit-level analysis (tracing how specific heads compose with each other across layers via the residual stream), and privileged vs. non-privileged bases (whether the head's own output basis is meaningful or just an artifact of how we're slicing things). A beginner looks at attention patterns and thinks they've found what a head "does" — an expert knows that the attention pattern is only half the picture; the value-times-output-weight matrix (the W_V W_O product) determines what information actually moves, and a head can attend to the right place while writing nearly nothing useful, or vice versa. The deeper expert worry is that heads may not be the right unit of analysis at all — if superposition means that the true "features" and "circuits" are spread across fractional combinations of heads, then any head-level story is a lossy projection onto the wrong basis, systematically misleading rather than merely incomplete.

The honest answer is that circuit boundaries are investigator-imposed abstractions, not natural joints in the model — the residual stream is a shared communication bus where every layer reads and writes, so any "circuit" you draw is a subgraph you've chosen to cut based on where causal effects drop below some threshold you've set. The IOI work handles this by tracing iteratively: they start from the logits, patch backward to find which heads matter, then ask what those heads' queries and keys depend on, finding a layered dependency structure (name-movers depend on S-inhibition heads, which depend on induction-like duplicate-token heads) — but the terminus is arbitrary, because you could keep tracing into the embeddings and positional encodings. Conmy et al.'s 2023 ACDC (Automatic Circuit DisCovery) paper tried to automate this with a threshold-based edge-pruning algorithm on the computation graph, and what they found implicitly reveals the problem: the "circuit" size and shape is sensitive to the KL-divergence threshold you choose, with no principled stopping criterion that falls out of the math itself. A more principled framing comes from thinking about minimal sufficient subgraphs — the smallest subgraph whose activation-patched output is statistically indistinguishable from the full model on the target behavior — but this is computationally intractable to find exactly and approximations tend to either over-include (everything matters a little) or under-include (missing upstream constructors). The deepest issue is that "where the circuit is" and "what the circuit does" are not independent questions: if you draw the boundary to exclude the upstream heads that build the Q/K subspace the downstream head operates in, you get a circuit description that is causally accurate but algorithmically incomplete — you've identified the executor but not the setup, which means your abstraction will fail to generalize to cases where the setup differs.

The core tool is path patching rather than activation patching: instead of replacing a head's full output, you intervene only on specific edges in the computation graph — patching the output of head A as it flows into head B's queries, but not into head C — which lets you test whether a head's contribution to a downstream component is load-bearing versus coincidental. Goldowsky-Dill et al.'s 2023 "Localizing Model Behavior with Path Patching" paper formalized this and showed that naive activation patching systematically over-attributes importance because replacing a head's output changes the residual stream for all downstream readers simultaneously, so you're measuring the head's effect plus all the downstream collateral, not the head's causal role in the specific circuit. A bystander head will show near-zero path-patching effect on the target behavior even when its activation patching effect looks meaningful — the activation patching effect was real but was mediated through some other downstream head that was doing the actual work. A second test is knockout asymmetry: for a genuine circuit member, ablating it should degrade performance roughly proportionally to its path-patching attribution; a bystander will show degradation that is disproportionately small relative to how much its activations correlate with behavior, because other heads compensate or the correlation was spurious. The residual worry, which nobody has fully solved, is redundancy: a model may have two heads that are both genuine circuit members doing the same computation as a robustness mechanism, so path-patching either one individually shows weak effects while ablating both shows catastrophic degradation — meaning single-head attribution methods will misclassify both as bystanders when they're actually a fault-tolerant pair.

Henighan et al.'s work on superposition and the broader Anthropic mechanistic interp program suggests that the same geometric pressure that causes superposition — packing more features than dimensions — also causes functional overlap, because if two heads learn to solve the same subproblem from different input cues, the model gets a free robustness bonus without any explicit incentive for it. The critical implication for interpretability is that there is no fact of the matter about which circuit the model "chose" in the sense of a deliberate selection: if redundant circuits co-exist, the model didn't pick one and implement the other as backup — both are simultaneously active and both contributed to gradient updates during training, so the causal history doesn't privilege either as the "real" solution. This breaks a common implicit assumption in circuit-level interpretability, which is that finding a sufficient circuit means you've found the algorithm — but if the model implements three overlapping sufficient circuits simultaneously, your clean story about the algorithm is actually a projection onto whichever circuit your particular activation patching setup happened to make most visible. Conmy et al.'s ACDC and subsequent work by Marks et al. on sparse circuit discovery both run into this: their recovered circuits vary depending on the prompt distribution used for evaluation, which is a signature of redundancy — different prompts activate different members of the redundant set, making the "circuit" an artifact of your evaluation slice rather than a stable property of the model.

Platonic similarity metrics like CKA (Centered Kernel Alignment), used extensively in vision models to compare representations across seeds and architectures, give you a continuous similarity score between representational geometries, but they're insufficient here because two circuits could have identical CKA scores while implementing different algorithms that happen to produce correlated outputs on your test set — you need functional equivalence under interventional probing, not just observational similarity. A stronger test is to take a causal intervention that disrupts circuit A (ablating its specific heads) and check whether circuit B compensates fully — if it does, and vice versa, you have evidence they're functionally intersubstitutable, which is necessary but not sufficient for same-algorithm status since two different algorithms could produce identical outputs on finite test sets by coincidence. The "different bases" framing points toward something like circuit alignment via weight-space symmetry: transformers have known symmetry groups (permutation of heads within a layer, rotation within head dimension for matched W_Q/W_K pairs) under which the function is invariant, and if two circuits are related by one of these symmetries they're provably the same algorithm — but the symmetry group of the full residual stream computation is poorly characterized and likely much larger than the obvious ones, making exhaustive alignment intractable. The honest current state is that nobody has a satisfying solution: Quirke and Barez's 2023 work on circuit replication across model seeds found that some circuits (induction heads) replicate almost exactly while others vary substantially, but the paper stops short of a formal criterion for when variation reflects different algorithms versus different bases, which remains an open problem that sits at the intersection of interpretability and the theory of program equivalence.

The induction head case is the clearest positive example: the bigram-to-skip-trigram computation they implement has a near-unique efficient solution given the transformer's architectural primitives (a previous-token head feeding a prefix-matching head via the residual stream), so SGD finds essentially the same circuit regardless of initialization — the algorithmic uniqueness and the circuit stability are both downstream of the same cause, which is that the task structure plus architecture leaves little room for variation. Conversely, behaviors that can be solved by multiple qualitatively different algorithms — like indirect object identification, which can exploit syntactic cues, positional cues, or token-identity cues depending on which the model happens to develop first — should show high cross-seed variance, and this is consistent with what Conmy et al. observe when they run ACDC across multiple GPT-2 checkpoints. The practical use of this as a proxy requires controlling for a confound: circuit instability could reflect measurement noise (your patching threshold, prompt distribution, or ablation method is finding different projections of the same stable circuit) rather than genuine algorithmic degeneracy, so you'd need to show that the variance persists under multiple independent recovery methods before concluding the underlying solution is genuinely non-unique. The most interesting implication, not yet systematically exploited, is that tracking circuit stability across training checkpoints within a single seed — not just across seeds — could reveal phase transitions in algorithmic commitment: a model might solve a task with high-variance proto-circuits early in training that consolidate into a stable low-variance circuit later, and the timing of that consolidation would tell you when and how the model "chose" among competing algorithmic strategies under the pressure of the full training distribution.

The competition between algorithms during consolidation is governed by early gradient amplification: whichever proto-circuit accumulates a small advantage in loss reduction first gets disproportionately stronger gradient signal, because the loss landscape is locally convex around nascent solutions and SGD accelerates toward them — this is the mechanistic story behind "grokking" (Power et al. 2022), where modular arithmetic solutions compete during training and the generalizing algorithm wins only after enough weight decay has penalized the memorization strategy sufficiently. Initialization luck matters most in the early training window before any circuit dominates: Nanda et al.'s 2023 grokking analysis showed that the Fourier-basis generalizing circuit and the memorization circuit coexist for a long period, with the generalizing circuit slowly accumulating efficiency advantages that only become decisive after thousands of steps — implying that an initialization that gave the memorizing circuit a larger head start would delay or potentially prevent consolidation onto the generalizing solution within a fixed compute budget. The key determinants of which algorithm wins are implicit regularization pressure (weight decay and dropout systematically favor circuits that achieve the same loss with smaller weight norms, which tends to favor compositional/generalizing solutions over memorization), data curriculum (early exposure to distributional diversity forces proto-circuits to generalize before they can overfit, biasing toward flexible algorithms), and architectural bottlenecks (attention head dimension and MLP width constrain which algorithms are even expressible efficiently, breaking symmetry between competing solutions). Intervention is possible and has been demonstrated: Anthropic's work on activation steering and more directly McDougall et al.'s 2023 work on copy suppression shows that you can amplify or suppress specific circuit components during training by injecting synthetic data that rewards or penalizes specific algorithmic strategies, effectively tilting the gradient landscape before consolidation occurs. The deeper unresolved question is whether steering interventions produce genuinely different algorithms or just surface rerouting — if you suppress the winning circuit early, does the model find the next-best algorithm in the loss landscape, or does it implement a superficially different but functionally equivalent circuit that achieves the same computation through a different basis, making your intervention cosmetic rather than substantive?
